approachQuestion.prompt:
Measure the closest repeated reading

Input: an array readings. Return the minimum positive index distance j−i among pairs i<j with readings[i]=readings[j]. Return −1 when no value repeats.

Example 1: readings = [8,3,8,8,3]. Output: 1. Example 2: readings = [4,7,4]. Output: 2. Example 3: readings = [1,2]. Output: −1. 0 ≤ n ≤ 200,000.

Constraints: input is immutable; all identifiers and numeric entries are signed 32-bit integers unless specified. Arithmetic uses signed 64-bit integers. Prefer the least expected running-time growth, then avoid unnecessary asymptotic auxiliary storage. Non-adversarial hashing of fixed-size integer keys/tuples has expected amortized constant cost.

options.text: Scan with a value-to-most-recent-index map. For a repeated value, minimize the answer with currentIndex−storedIndex, then overwrite its stored index.
options.feedback: For any fixed later position, its nearest equal predecessor is its best partner. Earlier predecessors cannot improve that distance.

options.text: Store a list of all indices for each value, then compare consecutive indices within every list.
options.feedback: This is correct and has equivalent total time, but retaining every occurrence is removable: only the most recent index per value is needed.

options.text: Store only each value’s first index, and minimize the distance from that index on repeats.
options.feedback: For [4,7,4,4], the true answer is 1 between indices 2 and 3; first-index distances miss it.

options.text: Sort the values and return the distance between equal neighbors in the sorted array.
options.feedback: Sorted-array positions are unrelated to original index distance. For [9,1,9], the correct distance is 2, not the sorted duplicate distance 1.

feedback.reason: Keep the most recent relevant position when the objective minimizes a distance.
details: Keep one latest index per value. At each position, if present, compare the distance to the saved latest index with the current minimum; then replace the saved index with this position. Process the entire input.
For occurrences at indices 1,4,5, the closest pair ends at 5 and starts at 4. Saving only the first occurrence would miss that distance, so overwrite with the latest index.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Measure the closest repeated reading — analyzed method”, n is input length and u is its number of distinct readings. Choose its time and auxiliary-space pair. Use the tightest standard bound for the worst legal input of size n, with expected time over non-adversarial hashing. Fixed-width integer and fixed-size tuple hash operations take expected amortized O(1); arithmetic, comparison and copying one integer take O(1). Auxiliary space excludes the supplied input and returned result, includes all maps, sets, temporary copies and call stacks. The method is iterative, with constant call-stack space.

options.text: Expected O(n + 1) time; O(u + 1) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: One latest index per distinct value avoids enumerating repeated-position pairs.
details: Keep the most recent relevant position when the objective minimizes a distance.
Each position causes one lookup and one update, so expected O(n+1) time.
One index for each of u distinct values plus constant scalar state uses O(u+1). This can be much smaller than storing all n positions.
“Expected O(n + 1) time; O(u + 1) auxiliary space.”: Correct under the stated expected/amortized hashing model.

“Expected O(n + 1) time; O(n + 1) auxiliary space even when u is bounded.”: The fixed method stores one latest index per distinct value, not all occurrence positions; O(n) is not the tight parameterized bound.
“Expected O(n + 1) time; O(1) space.”: The latest-index map can have u keys.
“Expected O(n² + 1) time; O(u + 1) space.”: It checks only the nearest predecessor via a lookup, not every earlier equal pair.
